title: Queues vs pub/sub vs event streams
description: Learn the differences between message queues, pub/sub systems, and event streams. Choose the right messaging pattern for your architecture.

data.text: Message-based architectures use different patterns for communication between services. Understanding the differences between queues, pub/sub, and event streams helps you choose the right tool for decoupling, scaling, and reliability.
Queues provide point-to-point messaging where each message is consumed by a single consumer. They're ideal for task distribution and workload balancing.

items: Competing consumers—multiple workers share the queue

data.title: Best For
data.text: Background job processing, task queues, email sending, image processing, any work that can be done asynchronously by a pool of workers.
Pub/sub provides one-to-many messaging where each message is delivered to all interested subscribers. It's ideal for event broadcasting and fan-out patterns.

items: Decoupled producers and consumers—no direct knowledge

data.title: Best For
data.text: Event notifications, cache invalidation, data synchronization, multi-consumer scenarios where different services need to react to the same event.
Event streams provide ordered, replayable logs of events. They're ideal for event sourcing, analytics, and systems that need to replay or reprocess events.

items: Replayable—consumers can re-read from any point
Retention—events kept for configurable time periods
Pull model—consumers control their read rate

data.title: Best For
data.text: Event sourcing, audit logs, real-time analytics, CDC (change data capture), systems that need to reconstruct state from history.
Your choice depends on your communication pattern and requirements.

items: Use queues for: Work distribution, async processing, load balancing
Use pub/sub for: Event broadcasting, notifications, loose coupling
Use event streams for: Event sourcing, replay, analytics, state reconstruction
Combine them: Queue + pub/sub for fan-out then process, Stream + queue for durability

data.title: Hybrid Approaches
data.text: Many systems use multiple patterns. For example, publish events to a stream for analytics, while also sending to a queue for immediate processing.
